name: Neurogenic Orthostatic Hypotension
aliases: Chronic orthostatic hypotension due to autonomic failure

prevalence.estimate: Varies by underlying cause; present in 30-80% of patients with synucleinopathies and other neurodegenerative autonomic disorders
prevalence.range: Neurogenic OH prevalence increases with age; ~5-30% of elderly depending on population studied

diagnosticCriteria.formalCriteriaName: American Autonomic Society / Consensus Statement on Neurogenic Orthostatic Hypotension

criteria.description: Sustained reduction of systolic blood pressure >=20 mmHg or diastolic >=10 mmHg within 3 minutes of standing or head-up tilt to at least 60 degrees
Insufficient compensatory heart rate increase (<15 bpm, or HR/SBP ratio <0.5 bpm/mmHg)
Evidence of underlying autonomic nervous system disease (neurodegenerative, autoimmune, or peripheral neuropathy)
Supine hypertension (systolic BP >=140 mmHg or diastolic >=90 mmHg)
Symptoms referable to cerebral hypoperfusion on standing

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Orthostatic hypotension (>=20/10 mmHg drop) with blunted heart rate response, in the setting of a known or demonstrable autonomic neuropathy
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Distinguished from non-neurogenic OH (caused by dehydration, medications, hemorrhage) by the blunted compensatory heart rate response. The neurogenic etiology indicates failure of the sympathetic noradrenergic system.

pathognomonic.symptomName: Sustained blood pressure drop on standing with inadequate compensatory heart rate increase
pathognomonic.notes: The blunted HR response distinguishes neurogenic from non-neurogenic OH

common.symptomName: Visual dimming or blurring on standing

common.notes: Suboccipital and paracervical ache from hypoperfusion of postural muscles

occasional.notes: BP drops further after eating due to splanchnic vasodilation

rare.symptomName: Transient ischemic attack symptoms on standing
Acute kidney injury from recurrent severe hypotension

laboratory: Supine and standing plasma norepinephrine: blunted or absent rise on standing (in postganglionic lesions, supine NE is low <100 pg/mL; in preganglionic, supine NE may be normal but fails to rise appropriately)
Screen for secondary causes: HbA1c, B12, TSH, serum protein electrophoresis
imaging: Cardiac MIBG: reduced in postganglionic (PAF, PD) vs. normal in preganglionic (MSA)
Brain MRI: may show findings of underlying neurodegenerative disease
genetic: Dopamine beta-hydroxylase deficiency: rare genetic cause (DBH gene mutations)
Genetics typically related to underlying disease (e.g., familial dysautonomia)
other: Active standing test or head-up tilt: sustained BP drop with blunted HR response
Valsalva maneuver: absent late phase II recovery and absent phase IV overshoot
QSART/thermoregulatory sweat test: may show sudomotor failure
24-hour ambulatory BP monitoring: characteristic nocturnal non-dipping or reverse dipping

distinguishingFeatures: POTS has excessive HR increase (>=30 bpm) without sustained BP drop
nOH has sustained BP drop with blunted HR response
NCS is episodic with reflex bradycardia/hypotension triggered by specific stimuli
nOH is chronic with consistent BP drop on every standing
Non-neurogenic OH has appropriate compensatory tachycardia (HR rise >15 bpm)
Non-neurogenic causes include dehydration, hemorrhage, medications
MSA has nOH as a feature but also has motor features (parkinsonism or cerebellar ataxia)
Isolated nOH without motor features may be PAF or early phenotype

redFlags: Falls with injury from orthostatic syncope
Rapid progression of autonomic failure (consider autoimmune or paraneoplastic cause)
New-onset severe nOH after starting or changing medications
Associated with progressive neurological deficits (evaluate for MSA, PD, DLB)
references: Gibbons CH, et al. The recommendations of a consensus panel for the screening, diagnosis, and treatment of neurogenic orthostatic hypotension and associated supine hypertension. J Neurol. 2017;264(8):1567-1582.
Freeman R, et al. Consensus statement on the definition of orthostatic hypotension, neurally mediated syncope and the postural tachycardia syndrome. Clin Auton Res. 2011;21(2):69-72.
Palma JA, Kaufmann H. Management of orthostatic hypotension. Continuum (Minneap Minn). 2020;26(1):154-177.
